Sheet Set · Object-Oriented Foundations

The List Is a Class

// using something you already know to learn classes, instances, and methods

You've been doing object-oriented programming since your very first my_list = [] — you just didn't have the vocabulary yet. Python's list is a built-in class: a blueprint. Every list you create is an instance of that class. And .append(), .sort(), and friends are methods — functions that belong to the class and act on one instance's data. This sheet uses the list you already understand to make those three words concrete.

Fig. 1 — one class, many instances, shared methods

Fig. 2 — the same class → instance → method idea, laid out as a full infographic

Foundation

Everything Is an Object

In Python, every value — not just lists — is an instance of some class. Click a value below to check.

01 type() and isinstance() — proving it click to expand +

Click a value to see what class it's an instance of.

click a value above ↑
everything_is_an_object.pypython 3
my_list = [1, 2, 3]

print(type(my_list))            # <class 'list'>
print(isinstance(my_list, list))  # True — my_list IS an instance of list
<class 'list'> True

[1, 2, 3] isn't just "a list" in some vague sense — it is literally an object built from the class named list. The square-bracket syntax is just a shortcut for calling that class.

The core idea

Class vs. Instance

A class is the blueprint — it defines what capabilities are available. An instance is one specific object built from that blueprint, holding its own data. Create two lists below and prove they don't share state.

02 Two instances of the same class, independent data click to expand +

cart_a and cart_b are both instances of list — same class, same available methods — but changing one never touches the other.

cart_a = list()
id(cart_a) → 0x7f001
empty
cart_b = list()
id(cart_b) → 0x7f002
empty
two_instances.pypython 3
cart_a = []   # a new, independent list instance
cart_b = []   # a completely separate list instance

cart_a.append("mouse")
print(cart_a)  # ['mouse']
print(cart_b)  # [] — untouched by cart_a's change
['mouse'] []

This is the whole point of instances: the class is shared (both are lists, both understand .append()), but the data is not.

03 Equality vs. identity — == and is click to expand +

Two different instances can hold equal data without being the same object. This distinction only makes sense once you think in terms of objects, not just values.

identity.pypython 3
list_a = [1, 2, 3]
list_b = [1, 2, 3]
list_c = list_a   # not a copy — another name for the SAME instance
click a check above ↑

== asks "do these hold the same values?" is asks "are these literally the same object in memory?" list_c = list_a doesn't create a new instance — it just gives a second name to the one that already exists.

Behavior

Methods — Functions That Belong to a Class

A method is a function defined inside a class, called on a specific instance using dot notation. Pick an instance below and call methods on it.

04 Dot notation — instance.method() click to expand +

Starting instance: numbers = [5, 3, 8, 1]. Every button below calls a method the list class provides — notice the pattern is always instance.method(...).

click a method button above ↑

Notice numbers.append(9) never mentions which list to modify by name inside the method itself — Python passes numbers in automatically as the object the method acts on. That's what "belongs to the instance" means in practice.

05 Classes are objects too click to expand +

Once you start looking, the pattern goes all the way down: list itself is an instance of another class called type.

turtles_all_the_way_down.pypython 3
print(type([1, 2, 3]))  # <class 'list'> — an instance's class
print(type(list))         # <class 'type'> — the class of the class
<class 'list'> <class 'type'>

You don't need this for everyday programming — but it's worth seeing once: in Python, classes aren't a separate kind of thing bolted onto the language. They're objects, just like everything else.

06 Naming conventions — CapWords vs. lowercase built-ins click to expand +

By convention, programmer-defined class names are capitalized, following the CapWords style (also called PascalCase) — each word starts with a capital letter, no underscores.

student_record.pypython 3
class StudentRecord:
    pass

However, Python's built-in collection types use lowercase names:

builtin_constructors.pypython 3
a = list()
b = []
d = dict()
s = set()

list is itself a built-in class — a = list() and b = [] both create a fresh list instance, just through different syntax. It just doesn't follow CapWords, because it predates that convention becoming standard: list, dict, set, str, int, and the other built-in types were named early in Python's history, alongside ordinary functions like len() and print(), before the community settled on capitalizing class names.

Click each name below to check it against convention.

click a name above ↑

Rule of thumb going forward

  • Writing your own class? Use CapWords: StudentRecord, ShoppingCart, BankAccount.
  • Calling a built-in type as a constructor? It'll be lowercase: list(), dict(), set(), str(), int().
  • Either way, you're doing the same thing — instantiating a class. The capitalization is a style convention (part of Python's PEP 8 guide), not a rule the language enforces.

Bringing it together

Writing Your Own Class

list is a built-in class — but the pattern (class → instance → method) is exactly the same one you'll use to write your own. Here's the smallest possible custom class, deliberately shaped just like the list examples above, and named the way StudentRecord was above.

07 A custom class, side by side with list click to expand +
shopping_cart.pypython 3
class ShoppingCart:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []              # each instance gets its own list

    def add_item(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)      # a method, just like .append() on list

cart_a = ShoppingCart()   # create instance 1
cart_b = ShoppingCart()   # create instance 2 — separate from cart_a

cart_a.add_item("mouse")
print(cart_a.items)   # ['mouse']
print(cart_b.items)   # [] — cart_b is untouched
['mouse'] []

Mapping the vocabulary

ConceptIn listIn ShoppingCart
ClasslistShoppingCart
Instancemy_list = []cart_a = ShoppingCart()
Method.append(x).add_item(x)
Per-instance datathe list's own elementsself.items

self is simply how a method refers to "the specific instance I was called on" — it's why cart_a.add_item("mouse") only ever changes cart_a, never cart_b. This is exactly the same mechanism that kept cart_a and cart_b separate back in Sheet 02, except now you can see the code that makes it happen.

Q3

tap to reveal

Q4
In a custom class's method, what does self refer to?
